html:
The Calusa were a Native American people of the southwest coast of Florida, who at the time of Spanish contact ruled most of south Florida. The map shows them in 1492 and 1500.

Unusually for a powerful chiefdom, they did not farm. Estuaries full of fish and shellfish fed them, and they built large mounds of shell, canals and towns on them. Their capital was at Mound Key in Estero Bay, where the paramount chief lived and received tribute from towns across the region.

The Calusa fought off the Spanish for decades. Juan Ponce de León was wounded by a Calusa arrow in 1521 and died soon after. In 1566 Pedro Menéndez de Avilés made a pact with the chief the Spanish called Carlos, but a Jesuit mission failed. In the 1700s disease and slave raids by Creek and Yamasee allies of the English destroyed them, and the last survivors are thought to have left for Cuba.
